title: Uneven resilience: Memorializing mass death in the El Paso–Juárez borderlands
abstract: This article investigates how two mass-fatality events in the El Paso–Ciudad Juárez borderlands—a 2019 mass shooting and a 2023 fire in a detention center—produced profoundly different memorial ecologies, and what these divergences reveal about the politics of resilience in a binational community. In El Paso, the idiom “El Paso Strong” channeled collective grief into sanctioned, commodified practices and durable forms of public memorialization. In Juárez, the deaths of migrants in state custody generated fragile, actively suppressed memorials, reflecting their exclusion from recognized modes of public mourning. Drawing on material culture studies, I treat these memorials as infrastructures whose forms, circulation, and durability reveal who is permitted access to public grief and who must mourn under conditions of precarity. I argue that these divergent memorial ecologies show how resilience in the borderlands is produced through bordering practices that distribute grievability unevenly across racialized and spatial categories.
